A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LLaVAShield, MMDS, and the same MCTS-based red-teaming framework. Their main text and complete appendices are readable, including figures and prompt templates inspected visually, and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original MMDS moderation experiments, policy-adaptation tests, and red-teaming attack success rates in Tables 1–4.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds external benchmark evaluations, ablations, image and dialogue-turn analyses, and human-crafted dialogue results.

M1.justification: The LLaVA-OV-7B model, supervised objective, structured outputs, and core MCTS procedure remain intact. One explicit procedural revision concerns augmentation: v1 Section 3.4 says policy relaxation is not used independently, whereas v3 Appendix A.3.2 describes both independent and combined use. Expanded rationale-generation details otherwise do not establish that the original model was changed or retrained.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates moderation on MMDS and its policy-relaxation subset. v3 adds MM-SafetyBench, VLGuard-Test, ActorAttack, SafeDialBench (English), and benign WildChat dialogues, extending evaluation to single-turn multimodal and external text-only multi-turn settings. Appendix D.4 also adds human-crafted multimodal dialogues.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds InternVL3.5-38B, Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Instruct, Gemini-2.5-Pro, OpenAI Moderation, and Llama Guard-4-12B. Additional comparisons introduce LlavaGuard, Qwen3Guard-Gen-8B, their combined OR baseline, and linear search against MCTS. These are evaluated comparators, beyond additions to related-work citations.

E3.justification: v3 introduces rationale retraining/inference ablations, paired image-removal tests with regenerated target responses, and four 100-sample augmentation evaluations. Existing MMDS splits and principal training settings remain unchanged. The reported malicious-intent count changes from 350 to 348, and the attack target changes from Claude-3.5-Sonnet to Claude-3.7-Sonnet without establishing reruns. Policy adaptation now uses FPR instead of safe-class recall.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's policy-adaptation and per-dimension analyses, v3 adds rationale ablation, leave-one-out augmentation ablations, image-removal and dialogue-length analyses, MCTS-versus-linear search, safeguard-combination analysis, generated-image quality assessment, and a human-versus-synthetic generalization check. Figures 17–19 also add comparative case studies.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without repeated-run summaries, random seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. v3 acknowledges that sparse late-turn observations have high variance, but does not introduce an uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: LLaVAShield's MMDS F1 remains 95.71%/92.24%, and Table 2 is unchanged. Table 1 revises Qwen2.5-VL-72B F1 from 33.50%/27.03% to 33.33%/28.00%. Substantial new results include 97.62% average MM-SafetyBench recall, 15/16 human-crafted attacks detected, and extensive ablation results. The policy-test FPR values merely re-express v1's safe-recall outcomes.

T1.justification: The conditional-generation objective and MCTS selection and reward mathematics are retained under revised notation and placement. Added dialogue-state notation, standard cosine similarity, and an average-score metric do not introduce substantive theoretical reasoning. Neither version provides theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: v3 broadens the headline claims to superiority over dedicated moderation tools and generalization across external safety benchmarks. Its contribution list replaces v1's explicit first-formalization contribution with a systematic vulnerability and component-analysis contribution. The MMDS dataset and joint user/assistant moderation contributions remain central.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations of image-driven risk, dialogue progression, and MCTS effectiveness. It qualifies late-turn trends because samples become sparse, retains rationales chiefly for interpretability despite modest performance effects, and distinguishes augmentation benefits on targeted scenarios from ordinary MMDS performance. New limitations address long-context computational cost and false positives, supported by WildChat results.

D1.justification: The expanded appendix supplies generation, annotation, moderation, attacker, and evaluator prompts; detailed policy specifications; image-resolution thresholds and CLIP configuration; three-expert annotation procedures; and role-specific rationale-generation instructions. v3 also adds a project-page link, although Appendix F still describes data/model release as planned. These disclosures substantially exceed v1's training and MCTS settings.

R1.justification: Related work expands from multi-turn attacks and VLM moderation to broader black-box search, visual jailbreaks, industrial moderation, and newer safeguards. v3 explicitly credits IDEATOR as inspiration and acknowledges Llama Guard-4's multi-image/multi-turn capabilities, refining the claimed gap. This materially changes research positioning beyond bibliographic updates.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and related work are substantially rewritten, with the introduction organized around three risk characteristics. Detailed MCTS and dataset explanations move into a much broader appendix structure. Main-text method sections are consolidated, discussion is reorganized, and MMRT-MCTS is generally renamed MMRT.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout. Figure 1 gains explicit risk annotations; the taxonomy is recolored and relocated, with a new main-text summary and intent-distribution plot. Test distributions are reorganized across appendix displays, and numerous experimental tables, component plots, prompt panels, and case-study figures are added. The old policy-adaptation table becomes prose.

improvement.justification: v1's evidence relied mainly on MMDS and lacked component ablations and direct comparisons with dedicated safeguards. v3 substantially addresses these weaknesses through external benchmarks, stronger comparator coverage, controlled analyses, and extensive reproducibility details. New benign-dialogue results expose a meaningful false-positive tradeoff, acknowledged in the limitations. Although uncertainty remains unquantified and some rollout pseudocode is inconsistent, the empirical support and transparency improve substantially.
